content: In settings with low syphilis prevalence, the difference in overtreatment between using a single on-site rapid syphilis test (RST, Strategy A) and a single on-site rapid plasma reagin (RPR, Strategy B) test is minimal, with approximately 9 more cases of overtreatment per 1,000 pregnant women when using the RPR strategy. However, in high-prevalence settings, the difference becomes more pronounced, favoring the RST strategy, with 30–50 fewer cases of overtreatment per 1,000 women compared to the RPR strategy. When comparing the combination of on-site RST followed by RPR (Strategy C) to the single on-site RPR test (Strategy B), the difference in overtreatment is negligible. Similarly, the difference in harms related to missed treatment between the single on-site RST (Strategy A) and the single on-site RPR (Strategy B) is small in low-prevalence settings (approximately 4 more missed cases per 1,000 women with the RPR strategy) but becomes moderate in high-prevalence settings (25–30 more missed cases per 1,000 women with the RPR strategy). The number of pregnant women screened appears to be slightly higher or similar with the single on-site RST strategy (Strategy A) compared to other strategies, with no significant differences observed across prevalence settings. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) emphasized the importance of prioritizing the detection of missed syphilis cases due to the severe adverse effects of untreated syphilis during pregnancy, including congenital syphilis and fetal death. While overtreatment may lead to minor side effects such as gastrointestinal symptoms, it was considered acceptable to some extent, though large-scale overtreatment was deemed undesirable. Although there is no direct evidence on the impact of different screening and treatment strategies on partner notification, the GDG agreed that using a sequence of tests (Strategy C) could potentially improve partner treatment rates. This is because additional confirmatory tests may increase confidence in positive results among both pregnant women and their partners. Cost-effectiveness modeling revealed that the total costs per 1,000 women screened were lowest with the RPR strategy in Tanzania and Zambia, while RST was the most cost-effective in Peru due to labor costs associated with RPR. Overall, the most cost-effective approach across all prevalence settings was the single on-site RST followed by treatment if positive (Strategy A). However, this strategy may incur higher costs in some settings. Although no studies directly assessed the equity impact of different strategies, it was noted that some pregnant women in certain countries might face direct costs for screening and treatment services. Despite this, screening rates were slightly higher with the single on-site RST strategy (Strategy A), suggesting that such costs may not significantly reduce equity. There were no studies comparing the acceptability of RST to RPR, but existing research indicated that both health workers and pregnant women were satisfied with RSTs due to their ease of use and reduction in clinic visits. Feasibility studies demonstrated that on-site tests have been successfully implemented in many countries, though a sequence of on-site tests may be unaffordable in some settings and require adequate provider training. The GDG concluded that using a single on-site RST followed by treatment if positive (Strategy A) or a sequence of RST followed by RPR and additional treatment doses if positive (Strategy C) could lead to higher treatment rates, fewer missed cases, and fewer instances of overtreatment compared to other strategies (e.g., Strategy B). In low-prevalence settings, the single on-site RST (Strategy A) and the sequence of tests (Strategy C) yielded similar results. However, in high-prevalence settings, fewer women were overtreated when using the sequence of tests (Strategy C). The single on-site RST strategy (Strategy A) was found to be cost-effective, feasible to implement, and acceptable to key stakeholders. Healthcare providers should receive training and information about syphilis prevalence in pregnant women and the risks of mother-to-child transmission. Pregnant women and their partners may require additional support when discussing partner treatment. Research priorities include trials comparing the sensitivity and specificity of different test sequences, as well as studies assessing outcomes such as partner notification, treatment, and long-term consequences of screening and treatment for mothers and infants.
